name: Lena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Brookfield, a 280-hectare farm owned by a co-operative of twelve local families. I'm up at half five to check the suckler herd, that's 90 beef cows and their calves, then I meet my team of four in the yard office over tea. Mornings are stock work, afternoons are the arable side: wheat, barley and field beans. I finish most days with an hour of paperwork, which I hate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love calving season, honestly, even the 3 a.m. ones, because a live calf on the straw is the best feeling I know. What wears me out is the co-op board meetings, twelve families with twelve opinions about the price of fertiliser. I'm 58, my knees aren't what they were, and I'm starting to count the years to my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: farming has seen plenty of shiny promises come and go. At the co-op meeting I'd tell them not to buy anything just because a salesman says AI on the box. Online I'd probably share something about how real farm work still needs real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not relaxed. The board has been talking about merging with the bigger co-op at Hallam, and that worries me more than any computer. If nothing changes with AI, I still have that, plus a pension that won't stretch far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on running the farm the way I do now, and keep using that chatbot now and then for grant forms. I'd put an extra 150 a month into savings, because João and I only have about four months put by. And I'd push the board to give me a straight answer on the merger before spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a little knot in my stomach about the merger. It feels like the weather: you can't stop it, you just watch the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the merger. What would it mean for your job if it went through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hallam already has a farm manager, a young man called Petr with a degree in data. Two managers for one bigger operation doesn't add up, and I'm the older one. They'd probably offer me a stockperson job, which I'd take, but it would be a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to João if the board told you that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make us both a cup of tea and say we'd planned for worse. João drives the school bus, so his wage is steady, and our kids are grown and paid for. I'd tell him a co-op that merges to survive is still better than one that sells to a big company.

say: Farming has seen **shiny promises** come and go before, and AI looks like another one.
Real farm work still needs **real people** in the yard every day.
think: The planned **merger with Hallam** worries me far more than any computer does.
My **pension** won't stretch far, so even a quiet world isn't a safe one for me.
do: Put an **extra 150 a month** into savings to grow our four-month cushion.
Press the board for a **straight answer** on the merger before spring.
Keep using the **chatbot** now and then for grant forms.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a knot in her stomach about the **merger**.
S0.quote: Two managers for one bigger operation doesn't add up, and I'm the older one.
fieldNote: Her real worry is **co-op consolidation**, not technology; AI barely registers in this picture.
She has already thought through taking a **pay cut** to stay on as stockperson.
Her husband's **steady bus wage** is the anchor she reaches for first.

steps.text: Add 150 a month to the household savings account
Keep managing the suckler herd and the arable rotation as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op needs to own these tools together, not let each family get picked off by a software company. At the regional farmers' union meeting I'd ask for training that's free for workers, not just owners. Online I'd say the people who do the work should get a share of the time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job is about half paperwork and planning now, so this would bite into the bit that makes me a manager. The board might decide software can do the planning and a cheaper stockperson can do the rest. The hands-on side would last longer, but that's not what pays manager wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the union's course on farm planning software in the first winter, so I'm the one who runs it, not the one it replaces. I'd ask the board to put my contract to 2031 in writing. And I'd keep the extra savings going and start reading our pension statement properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sad, if I'm honest. I spent thirty years learning to read a field, and now a programme reads a satellite picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, who's 24 and does most of our spraying records and ordering. That's exactly the kind of work the software would swallow. I'd want the co-op to move Sam onto the livestock side, where there's still real need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op should own the tools together. Would the board agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them would, the older half wouldn't. Mr Okafor would say we've managed fine with a notebook since 1970. I'd have to show them the numbers, and I'd probably need the chatbot to help me make the numbers look good.

say: The co-op should **own the tools together** so no family gets picked off alone.
Workers deserve **free training** and a share of the **time saved**.
think: About **half my job** is planning and paperwork, which is the part software takes.
The board could swap a manager for **software plus a stockperson**, which would cost me my wage.
do: Take the union's **farm software course** in the first winter.
Ask the board for a **written contract** running to 2031.
Read the **pension statement** properly and keep up the extra savings.
feel: **Sad** that thirty years of reading fields could be matched by a satellite picture.
S1.quote: I spent thirty years learning to read a field, and now a programme reads a satellite picture.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that the **thinking half** of her role is what earns manager pay.
Her answer is **collective**: co-op ownership, union training, protecting younger staff.
She worries more for **Sam, the young worker**, than she admits worrying for herself.

steps.text: Take the farmers' union course on farm planning software this winter
Ask the co-op board for a written contract to 2031
Use the chatbot to build cost figures for the board

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need governments to step in, and fast. Two years isn't enough for anyone to plan, least of all farm workers. I'd join whatever the union organises, a march, a letter, anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of a manager's job by 2029, because the planning and grant work goes on day one. The robots for the cattle wouldn't come till about 2031, when I'm 63, so I might cling on as a stockperson for those years. After that, I honestly don't know who hires a 63-year-old to do what a robot does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with João and work out what we'd live on if my wage halved. I'd stop the holiday we'd planned for Clara's wedding year and put that money into savings. I'd ask the union about early pension access, and I'd offer the board to stay on hands-on work at a lower rate so they keep me till the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but in a cold, practical way. Like when a cow is in trouble at night and you don't have time to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between the thinking AI coming first and the robots three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years between the thinking AI and the robots are my bridge. The office side of my job goes in 2028, but somebody still has to pull a calf and fix a fence until 2031. If I can keep my hands busy for three years, I get to 63 and my pension's a bit closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Clara about her wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to go ahead, but smaller. Clara's a vet nurse, and I'd tell her the animals will still need people for a while, so to keep her head down and save. A wedding in the village hall is still a wedding.

say: Governments must **step in fast**; two years is no time for farm workers to plan.
I'd join any **union action** going, from letters to marches.
think: The **manager's job** would likely go by 2029, when planning moves to software.
The **cattle work** might hold until 2031, but nobody hires a 63-year-old after that.
do: Cancel the planned **family holiday** and put the money into savings.
Ask the union about **early pension access** in the first month.
Offer the board **cheaper hands-on work** to stay on until robots arrive.
feel: **Frightened** but practical, like a night emergency with a cow in trouble.
S2.quote: The three years between the thinking AI and the robots are my bridge.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year robot gap** as a bridge to her pension, not a reprieve.
She accepts a **pay cut** almost instantly, which shows how she ranks security above status.
Even in crisis she plans a **smaller wedding**, not a cancelled one.

steps.text: Cancel the planned holiday and move that money into savings
Ask the union about drawing her pension early
Offer the board hands-on stock work at a lower rate until 2031
Join the union's campaign for government help for farm workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so there's no excuse for anyone not to plan, including the government. At the union I'd push for a fund to retrain farm workers before 2031, not after. I'd tell friends this is the time to talk, not to shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for me. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots come for the stock work. If the co-op keeps me as manager till 2031 and as a stockperson after, I could reach a sort of retirement without falling off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd raise our savings by 200 a month and pay off the last of the car loan within two years. I'd volunteer to run the co-op's switch to planning software, so I'm the person who knows it. I'd also train Sam on the cattle, so someone young is ready when I step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It feels like a long walk downhill rather than a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be grabbing what I could. With five I can do it properly: learn the software, pass on what I know, and leave on my own terms. That matters to me, leaving with my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from when your wage stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My co-op pension, João's bus pension, and whatever we've saved. It won't be much, maybe two thirds of what we live on now. We'd sell the second car and grow more of our own veg.

say: We've been **warned five years** ahead, so nobody, government included, has an excuse.
The union should fund **retraining before 2031**, not after.
think: Five years is **just about enough** to reach a soft retirement.
Manager to 2031, then **stockperson to 2034**, gets me to 66 without a cliff.
do: Raise savings by **200 a month** and clear the car loan within two years.
Volunteer to **run the switch** to planning software.
Train **Sam on the cattle** so someone young is ready.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, like a long walk downhill.
S3.quote: Five years is just about enough for me. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots come for the stock work.
fieldNote: She treats five years as time to **leave with dignity**, not just to survive.
Her retirement income falls to roughly **two thirds**, which keeps the worry real.
She **steps toward the software** rather than away, typical of a steady adopter once it's proven.

steps.text: Raise savings by 200 a month and clear the car loan
Volunteer to lead the co-op's move to planning software
Push the union for a farm worker retraining fund before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it arguing. At the co-op I'd say let's plan the next generation of Brookfield now. Online I'd probably post about pensions, because nobody my age thinks about them till too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, more or less. I'm 68 when the thinking AI arrives and 71 when the robots come, and I'll have retired by then. My worry is Clara and Rui, who'll be in their forties when the world turns over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am and aim to retire at 65 as planned. I'd put a bit extra into the pension each year. And I'd help the co-op hire and train a younger manager by 2030, so the hand-over is clean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me, uneasy about my kids. It's a strange split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rui, your son in the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rui's an electrician, and I'd tell him robots still need wiring and fixing, so he's in a decent spot. I'd tell him to learn the robot side of his trade now. He'd roll his eyes, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the co-op survive in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if it buys the machines together. A small family can't afford a robot herdsman, but twelve families can share one. That's what co-ops were invented for.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and we shouldn't waste it arguing.
People my age should sort their **pensions now**, not later.
think: I'll have **retired by 2039**, so the robots mostly miss me.
My real worry is **Clara and Rui**, who'll be in their forties.
do: Keep working and **retire at 65** as planned.
Help the co-op **hire a younger manager** by 2030.
Add a little **extra to the pension** each year.
feel: **Calm** about herself and **uneasy** about her grown children.
S4.quote: A small family can't afford a robot herdsman, but twelve families can share one. That's what co-ops were invented for.
fieldNote: Her **age** turns the decade into a buffer, so her worry shifts to her children.
She sees **shared ownership** as the answer to costly machines.
Her tone is lighter here, but she still names the **pension gap**.

steps.text: Keep running Brookfield until retiring at 65
Help the co-op recruit and train a younger manager by 2030
Pay a little extra into the pension each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it takes the office side of my job before I've had time to plan. What would help is a proper bridge for older farm workers, like early pension access at 60 if your job goes to a machine. And free training run through the union, not sold by the companies making the software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Whatever happens, somebody has to care whether a cow is in pain, and I'm not sure a robot cares about anything. I'd like that written into the rules before it's too late.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens, somebody has to care whether a cow is in pain, and I'm not sure a robot cares about anything.
portrait: Lena, 58, manages a **co-op-owned mixed farm** with 90 suckler cows and a team of four.
She is progressive, a **union supporter**, and uses a chatbot only for grant forms.
Her biggest pressure before AI is a **possible merger** that could cost her the manager's job.
In every scenario she reaches for **collective answers**: shared machines, union training, protecting younger staff.
Her mood depends on **timing**: two years scares her, ten years mostly passes her by.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it takes the planning side of her job before she can prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Early pension access** at 60 for farm workers whose jobs go to machines.
**Free training** run through the union rather than sold by software firms.
